title: Why did Africans come to Tudor England?

review.note: Built from Mr Garry's own lessons for this unit (2026–27 scheme of work). Check wording against the lesson PowerPoints before relying on it.

learn.intro: Africans lived in England long before the 20th century. Historians have found hundreds of named Africans in Tudor and Stuart records, from royal trumpeters to sailors, divers and seamstresses. This topic asks why they came, using the push and pull factors that the Pearson GCSE Migrants in Britain course uses for every period.

sections.title: 1. An African presence in Tudor England

blocks.p: Africans lived in Tudor towns such as London, Southampton, Plymouth and Bristol. Miranda Kaufmann has documented over 360 named Africans in Britain between 1500 and 1640, and Onyeka Nubia argues that some were born in England.

Historians find them in parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials), royal accounts, court cases, letters and wills. Words used at the time included "blackamoore", "Moor" and "Ethiopian". These are historical terms, and they did not always mean the same thing.
This was part of England's growing international role: more trade, exploration and contact with Africa, Spain, Portugal and the Mediterranean.
Reasons were often mixed. Historians group them into push and pull factors:

ul: Royal and noble households: Catherine of Aragon arrived from Spain in 1501 with a household that included Africans. Spain and Portugal already had large African populations.
Trade: merchants traded with Morocco, West Africa and the Iberian peninsula. Mary Fillis came from Morocco around 1583.
Skills: Africans brought skills that were valued, such as music (John Blanke, trumpeter) and diving (Jacques Francis).
Escaping Spanish slavery: Diego escaped Spanish enslavement in Panama and joined Francis Drake in 1572.
Privateering: English ships attacked Spanish and Portuguese shipping, and Africans on board sometimes ended up in England.

blocks.p: Some came by choice, some were brought by others, and some escaped. A single person's journey could involve all three.

sections.title: 3. How historians know: Kaufmann and Onyeka

blocks.p: Two historians have shaped how we understand Black Tudors:

ul: Onyeka Nubia, "Blackamoores" (2013): argues Africans lived across urban England, were often employed for specialist skills, and were not automatically at the bottom of society.
Miranda Kaufmann, "Black Tudors" (2017): tells the stories of ten individuals, showing that Africans were baptised, married, paid wages and gave evidence in court.

blocks.p: Both use archives, but records only survive for some people, and are usually written by others. Asking whose voice survives is part of the history.

timeline.event: Catherine of Aragon arrives from Spain; Africans are among her household.
John Blanke, "the blacke trumpet", appears in royal accounts.
The Mary Rose sinks; Jacques Francis later dives on the wreck.
Diego joins Francis Drake at Nombre de Dios, Panama.
Mary Fillis arrives in London from Morocco.
A Privy Council letter allows Caspar van Senden to take Africans abroad, only with their masters' consent; the scheme fails.

misconceptions.wrong: There were no Black people in England before the 20th century.
misconceptions.right: Hundreds of Africans are recorded in Tudor and Stuart England.

misconceptions.wrong: All Africans in Tudor England were enslaved.
misconceptions.right: Many were free, waged and baptised; English law did not clearly recognise slavery.

misconceptions.wrong: Africans only came because they were forced.
misconceptions.right: Reasons included royal service, trade, skills and escape from Spanish slavery.

misconceptions.wrong: Elizabeth I deported all Africans in 1596.
misconceptions.right: The 1596 scheme needed masters' consent and failed; Africans stayed.

sources.title: Miranda Kaufmann, "Black Tudors: The Untold Story" (2017)
sources.origin: Written by a historian who researched records such as parish registers, court cases and royal accounts.
sources.purpose: To tell the life stories of ten Africans in Tudor and Stuart England.
sources.usefulness: Built from named individuals in archives. Kaufmann has documented over 360 Africans in Britain between 1500 and 1640. Each life is known only from the records that survive.

sources.title: Onyeka Nubia, "Blackamoores: Africans in Tudor England, their Presence, Status and Origins" (2013)
sources.origin: Written by a British historian after about ten years studying around 250,000 documents.
sources.purpose: To show that Africans were present across Tudor England and to challenge the idea that they were all slaves or outsiders.
sources.usefulness: Argues many Africans had valued skills and that a significant minority were born in England. Like any interpretation, its arguments should be weighed against the evidence.

sources.text: Kaufmann explains that she found records of over 360 Africans living in Britain between 1500 and 1640. They appear in baptism and burial registers, wage lists and court records, and worked as musicians, sailors, divers, servants and craftspeople in towns such as London, Bristol and Plymouth.

questions.label: Teacher-created practice question
questions.q: "Africans came to Tudor England mainly because of royal service." How far do you agree?
questions.asks: Weigh royal service against trade, skills, privateering and escape.
steps: Explain at least two other reasons with named people.
questions.plan: 2 minutes planning, 9 minutes writing, 1 minute checking.

model.t: Royal service was only partly the main reason, because Africans came for many different reasons.
John Blanke was paid as a royal trumpeter from 1507, but Diego came after escaping Spanish slavery in 1572, and Mary Fillis arrived from Morocco around 1583 through trade links.
This means royal courts explain some arrivals, but trade and conflict with Spain explain more of the later ones.
Therefore there was no single main reason; it changed across the Tudor period.

full: P: Royal service was the main reason to a large / some extent…
some: P – Topic sentence with a qualifier (blue): One key reason … / To a large extent … / On the other hand …
E – Precisely selected evidence (purple), in order with time connectives (green): At the start … / Later … / Eventually … / Finally …
E – Explain with arguing connectives (red): However … / This was more important because … / In contrast …
J – Judgement: This shows that … / Overall, the most important reason was … / Therefore, I agree to a large/limited extent …
